stories.headline: Trump rallies New York crowd for Republican Bruce Blakeman's bid to replace Gov. Kathy Hochul
stories.note: Trump headlined a Syracuse rally Friday night, pitching Bruce Blakeman as the man to flip New York's governorship from Kathy Hochul.
body: President Trump went back to his home state Friday night for a rally in Syracuse, making Republican Bruce Blakeman's run against Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul the main event as the midterms near.

Trump went after Hochul on New York's high taxes, steep utility bills and public safety, and said Blakeman could turn the state around with more domestic energy and lower costs for families. He promised to back Blakeman from the White House if he wins.

He also pointed to Micron's planned $100 billion chip complex in central New York, which the company says should create about 50,000 jobs statewide. Blakeman joined him onstage, promising tax and utility cuts and a friendlier climate for business, saying the state has to treat business "not as the enemy, but as a partner."

Trump also boosted GOP House hopefuls Kailee Buller in the 22nd District and Anthony Constantino in the open 21st, and former boxing champ Mike Tyson made a surprise appearance onstage. Trump urged the crowd to vote as if he were on the ballot himself.

Why it matters: A presidential rally in upstate New York signals Republicans see a real shot at the governor's mansion and at least two House seats in a deep-blue state, putting Hochul and Democrats on defense on their home turf.

stories.headline: Letitia James stumped by debate question while GOP rival delivers 'zinger for the ages'
stories.note: Letitia James froze when asked to name a past attorney general she admires, and GOP challenger Saritha Komatireddy shot back that James "only admires herself."
body: In Thursday's New York attorney general debate, Democratic AG Letitia James went silent for several seconds when a moderator asked her to name a former state attorney general she admired, with Spectrum News' Errol Louis prodding her with "Tick tock."

Her Republican challenger, former federal prosecutor and ex-DEA chief of staff Saritha Komatireddy, jumped in to say James "only admires herself." Komatireddy then named former GOP AG Dennis Vacco as her own pick, while James eventually named Democrat Bob Abrams.

Conservative strategist Steve Guest called the line a debate zinger for the ages, and Rensselaer County Executive Steve McLaughlin said the moment showed James has no feel for the office. Komatireddy's campaign said New Yorkers deserve a real prosecutor.

James' campaign countered that she spent the debate explaining to her opponent how the office really works and was glad to name Abrams. Trump, a longtime target of James' legal actions, endorsed Komatireddy in August.
Why it matters: James is one of Trump's most prominent legal foes, and a viral stumble in the campaign's final stretch gives Republicans fresh ammunition in a race they're eager to make competitive.

stories.headline: Trump says Rogers 'completely obliterated' El-Sayed in debate
stories.note: Trump declared Mike Rogers the clear winner of Thursday's Michigan Senate debate against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.
body: President Trump said Michigan Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers "completely obliterated" Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in their Thursday night debate, posting on Truth Social just after midnight Friday.

Trump, who has endorsed Rogers, praised him as a winner and harshly attacked El-Sayed's patriotism, while reminding voters he carried Michigan himself. Rogers served in the U.S. House from 2001 to 2015 and narrowly lost the 2024 Senate race to Elissa Slotkin.

El-Sayed's campaign didn't respond to Fox News Digital. In a statement a day earlier, El-Sayed accused Trump of using his name and faith to distract from high prices at the pump, the grocery store and the doctor's office.
Why it matters: Michigan's open Senate seat is one of the GOP's best pickup chances, and Republicans are framing El-Sayed, a progressive, as too far left for a swing state.

stories.headline: James Talarico resurfaces after extended absence as his campaign pushes back
stories.note: Texas Democrat James Talarico finally reappeared after nearly two weeks off the trail, after Trump and Ken Paxton spent days asking where he went.
body: Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico showed up Friday at the Austin City Limits festival after almost two weeks with no in-person campaign events, ending days of questions about where he'd been.

His last public event was a Sept. 26 press conference in Carrollton about gas prices, followed by a New York City fundraiser on Sept. 28. The campaign said he came down with a bad case of the flu, and his spokesman joked online that Talarico was "still alive and meeting with voters."

Republicans pounced. Trump called him "MISSING IN ACTION" on Truth Social and questioned how the flu could take 12 days, while his GOP opponent, Attorney General Ken Paxton, asked a San Antonio crowd, "Where is James Talarico?"

The campaign argued the gap was closer to nine days, since he joined a Sept. 30 Zoom call with a Hispanic business group, and said he had done more than 100 events before getting sick. He's expected back on a full schedule ahead of an Oct. 14 CNN town hall.
Why it matters: Losing nearly two weeks in the home stretch of a closely watched Texas Senate race handed Paxton and Trump an easy line of attack and cost Talarico valuable time with voters.

stories.headline: Former MN state trooper tears into Dems as Somali gang violence terrorizes Minnesota: 'Where is Ilhan Omar?'
stories.note: GOP challenger John Nagel, a 30-year state trooper, is hammering Ilhan Omar and Minnesota Democrats for going quiet as gang violence rattles Twin Cities suburbs.
body: John Nagel, a Republican who spent 30 years as a Minnesota state trooper, is blaming Rep. Ilhan Omar and state Democrats for letting gang violence grow in the Twin Cities. He's running against Omar in Minnesota's 5th District.

Recent incidents include two teens shot outside an Eden Prairie high school football game and more than 100 shell casings found in a Bloomington neighborhood. "Where is Ilhan Omar in all of this?" Nagel asked, saying he hasn't seen her at community meetings or offering help.

Nagel also faulted Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, Gov. Tim Walz and AG Keith Ellison, arguing soft-on-crime policies have emboldened gang members. Ramsey County Sheriff Bob Fletcher said this week that failing to hold offenders accountable is a big part of the problem and urged tougher prosecution of juveniles.

Moriarty's office said no Bloomington cases have been sent for charges yet but would be reviewed. An 18-year-old was charged Friday in the Eden Prairie shooting, and Moriarty said he will be held accountable. Nagel says the answer is enforcing existing laws, including a gang task force.

Why it matters: Public safety is a top midterm issue, and Republicans are using rising suburban violence to press Omar and Minnesota Democrats on crime in a state where Walz's leadership is already under fire.

stories.headline: Denver, Boulder ignored ICE detainers for migrants with child abuse, assault arrests, House GOP report reveals
stories.note: A new House Judiciary report says Denver and Boulder ignored ICE detainers for illegal immigrants arrested for child sex assault, child abuse and assault.
body: Rep. Jim Jordan's House Judiciary Committee released a 25-page report Friday accusing the top prosecutors in Denver and Boulder of helping illegal immigrants accused of crimes slip past ICE, and naming some of those cases for the first time.

The list includes a Venezuelan man arrested for sexual assault on a child, a Mexican national arrested in Boulder for child abuse, and at least four people arrested for domestic violence in Denver whose ICE detainers were ignored, according to the report.

Investigators say Denver gave ICE as little as one to two hours' notice before releasing a suspected Tren de Aragua member, who later assaulted an officer when agents tried to arrest him. The report also says both offices weigh immigration consequences when deciding charges, and that Boulder's DA bars information sharing with ICE.

Denver DA John Walsh said his office prosecuted several of the listed cases, and that ICE deported one suspect over its objection. Boulder DA Michael Dougherty called the report "a political stunt to sway voters before the midterm elections." Fox noted that ignoring a detainer doesn't always mean a suspect was released.

Why it matters: The findings give Republicans fresh evidence for their case against sanctuary policies weeks before the midterms, and put Colorado Democrats on the defensive over immigration and public safety.

stories.headline: 'Thrill killer' and desert executioner — meet the dozens of criminals Dem AG backed for parole: 'No brainer'
stories.note: A Fox review finds Nevada AG Aaron Ford, the Democrat running for governor, voted for clemency for 30 convicted murderers, including a so-called thrill killer.
body: Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford, the Democrat trying to unseat Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, voted to pardon or significantly cut the sentences of 30 people convicted of murder during his nearly eight years in office, according to a Fox News Digital review of pardon hearings.

In Nevada, clemency is decided by a board made up of the governor, attorney general and state Supreme Court justices. Ford backed parole eligibility for Michael Cu, who killed a 16-year-old execution-style in the desert in 1996 to steal his car's rims, over Lombardo's objection.

He also supported a commutation for Anthony Amati, whom prosecutors called a "thrill killer" for gunning down a 22-year-old Pizza Hut worker, and called parole eligibility for a man who stabbed a 17-year-old to death a "no-brainer." He backed clemency for a man who killed his victim with a cinder block, though the board denied it.

Ford is already under fire for supporting clemency for a man who killed a pregnant woman while out on bail. His campaign highlights his record as the state's top law enforcement officer. His office and campaign did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Why it matters: Nevada's governor's race is one of the most competitive of the cycle, and Ford's clemency votes give Lombardo and Republicans a sharp contrast on crime against his tough-on-crime pitch.
